title: Revolution speed and a 2011 claim
claim: Faster communication makes little difference to how quickly regimes fall: Egypt in 2011 took 17 days and Czechoslovakia in 1989 took 23.
verdict: The warning against equating communication speed with political speed holds up. The gap was six days, not five; neither two cases nor this selected wider comparison establishes that technology has no effect.

title: Literally: how close was I in 2011?
claim: In 2011 I argued that literally primarily intensifies, including factually true expressions, and that complaints about its misuse ran ahead of the evidence. How much survives a new check?
verdict: Right about established emphatic usage and overlapping functions; too categorical about register and grammar. The old frequency comparisons and claims about confusion remain unproved.

title: Do political hawks kill political doves?
claim: Political hawks and doves never acquire other bird behaviour, especially hawks hunting or killing doves; this is unusual because most public metaphors are elaborated.
verdict: My 2011 post overstated the lack of elaboration: feathers, calls, flight and a chase image existed. Killing or eating political doves remains unfound here, and the claim about most metaphors is untested.

title: Which scripts were deciphered, and where could AI agents help?
claim: Decipherment required combinations of evidence and iterative tests. Which parts could an AI agent automate?
verdict: Every accepted language recovery in this sample had a readable parallel or key, including names, or a known language or close relative, usually both. Names were the usual way in. No agent advantage has been demonstrated.

title: Canals and nuclear: smaller booms, long earnings and expensive failures
claim: British canals and civil nuclear power may fill gaps in the historical AI investment comparison; nuclear revenues would be very small.
verdict: Canal period-average spending was about 0.2% of GDP; the retrieved US nuclear series reached about 0.5%, with incomplete national coverage. Nuclear revenue was substantial at operating assets: the very-small-revenue guess is wrong as a general description. Revenue still has to cover construction, operation, financing and replacement.

title: AI spending, railway booms and the revenue test
claim: There is no twentieth-century US precedent for the infrastructure investment share; AI investment is likely to pay off if revenue keeps growing at the current pace or a little slower.
verdict: A close twentieth-century precedent: US railways reached 2.19% of GDP in 1910, just below the reproduced 2.3% global-company proxy. Fast revenue growth and estimated in-service cost coverage support optimism, conditional on asset life, costs and future demand.

title: Did work change more from 1900 to 1969 than from 1957 to 2026?
claim: 2026 is similar to 1957 in a way that 1969 was not from 1900.
verdict: True only when work is counted in the job categories of 1950: then 1900–1970 changed 1.3 to 1.6 times as much as 1950–2024 or 1960–2024. Counted in today's finer categories, the later span changed about as much, and women's work, college, professional work and immigration changed more.

title: Can a cake be sickly?
claim: Can “sickly” describe food and other inanimate things, before a noun or after a verb, as the only adjective? Is there a British–American difference?
verdict: Both uses occur without another adjective; the American sample is too sparse to establish a British–American difference.

title: Could AI control more wealth by 2035 than humans do today?
claim: davidad predicts that by 2050 AI will control more wealth than humans currently control; Dominik suggests 2035.
verdict: 2035 is plausible as an aggressive scenario for delegated capital allocation. Historical transitions do not establish a global wealth crossover or support almost-sure confidence.

title: Is only 1 of 270 jobs from 1950 obsolete?
claim: Only 1 job out of 270 in the 1950 census is now obsolete (elevator operator)
verdict: The number comes from a paper that counted jobs eliminated by automation, not jobs that are obsolete. At least 15 more 1950 jobs are gone, many more collapsed, and most of today's work did not exist in 1950, so the claim understates how much work has changed.
